newsitem.title: UK: Report recommends changes in Kenyan legal system.
newsitem.headline: Report recommends changes in Kenyan legal system.

text.p: An independent report into the Kenyan legal system has recommended sweeping changes after discovering widespread corruption and human rights abuses.

William Goodhart, one of the authors of the International Bar Association (IBA) report, told a news conference on Tuesday its primary concerns were the independence of the judiciary in Kenya and the harassment of lawyers.
"The justice system is thought to lack independence," he said. "There is a widespread belief that many of the judges are willing to take a pro-government line."
Goodhart said that corruption, at various levels, was also a major worry along with proposed legislation on the freedom of the press and the registration of political parties and other societies.
"Corruption is rife among court staff and is strongly suspected to exist among some magistrates and a few of the higher judiciary," the report said.

Goodhart and Phineas Mathale Mojapelo, a former president of the Black Lawyers' Association of South Africa, spent a week in Kenya last November at the invitation of the chairman of the country's Law Society.
Their report, which was presented simultaneously in Pretoria and Nairobi, was presented to the government of President Danial arap Moi.
"There is a great need for the executive arm of the government to distance itself and to allow greater space for the independence of the judiciary," Mojapelo said in a statment.
The report called for changes in the appointment of a chief justice, the establishment of a commission to investigate and weed out corruption and the recruitment of more judges from private practice.
It also urged the government to speed up appeal hearings and to review the role of the attorney-general and pre-trial procedures.
Turning to the question of human rights, Goodhart emphasised that Kenya was by no means the worst country in Africa but improvements were needed.

The report criticised the trial of radical politician and government opponent Koigi wa Wamwere who was jailed in 1995 for robbery. It described his 18-month trial as the most serious abuse of the criminal process in Kenya in recent years.
"Koigi and two of his co-defendants were convicted in spite of the extreme weakness of the prosecution evidence," the report concluded.

It urged the government to investigate all cases of suspected torture and to prosecute those responsible, and to follow the recommendations in the Amnesty International Report on Torture in Kenya that was published in December 1995.

"I hope that the relevant authorities in Kenya will look at the report and use it as a guide for the improvement of the human rights situation within the legal system and the judiciary in the country," said Mojapelo. REUTER
